profile.behavior: Forages deliberately in foliage, often high in the canopy; eats insects and wild fruits, and gives a distinctive chick-burr call.
field_marks: Medium-sized, compact songbird with a fairly long, straight-to-slightly pointed bill
Breeding male has a vivid scarlet-red head and body
Breeding male shows sharply contrasting jet-black wings and tail
Female, immature, and nonbreeding male are yellowish to olive-green with dark wings and tail
Dark, rounded eye; slender dark legs and feet
Long, dark tail extends well beyond the folded wings
profile.habitat: Primarily mature deciduous and mixed forests; also uses forest edges, younger woodland, and evergreen forest during the nonbreeding season.

sources.title: Scarlet Tanager Overview — All About Birds, Cornell Lab of Ornithology

findings: Species identity is correct: the plate depicts a breeding male Scarlet Tanager, Piranga olivacea, with the diagnostic scarlet head and body contrasting with black wings and tail. Cardinalidae is the current family assignment used by Cornell.

The measurement lines are accurate: “Length 16–17 cm,” “Wingspan 25–29 cm,” and “Weight 23.5–38 g” agree with the published ranges; Cornell rounds the mass to 23–38 g, while Animal Diversity Web gives 23.5–38 g.

The body-length diagram is internally consistent: 16 cm is at the bottom, 17 cm is at the top, values increase upward, the endpoints agree with the printed range, and exactly four evenly spaced unlabeled interior ticks divide the range into five proportional segments. “SCHEMATIC – NOT TO SCALE” clearly prevents interpreting it as the printed specimen’s physical scale.

The habitat text—“Mature deciduous & mixed forests; edges, young woodland; evergreen forest in nonbreeding season.”—is supported by the verified habitat accounts and contains no material spelling, number, omission, duplication, or word-order error.

The behavior text—“Deliberate foliage forager, often high in canopy; insects & wild fruits; chick-burr call.”—accurately reflects deliberate foliage foraging in tall trees, an insect-and-fruit diet, and the distinctive chick-burr call.

All five field-mark lines are valid. In particular, “Thick, blunt-tipped bill” and “Short, broad dark tail” agree with Cornell’s direct identification description; the proposed research-pass alternatives describing a fairly long pointed bill and a long tail are not supported by that source.

The primary specimen has appropriate compact, stocky proportions, a large rounded head, dark rounded eye, thick pale horn-colored bill, scarlet breeding plumage, black folded wing, dark tail, and two slender dark legs with grasping feet. The profile-obscured far wing does not create a duplicate or missing-anatomy defect.

The bill is closed and both mandibles converge consistently from their common base to a co-terminal tip in the primary specimen and detached head study. Unequal mandible projection is not established as a Scarlet Tanager field mark by the verified sources, so no projection correction is warranted.

The detached wing and detached head are clearly supplementary studies and do not appear attached to the primary specimen. Their plumage and bill treatment remain consistent with the main bird and the references.

The palette labels—“scarlet,” “jet black,” “olive green,” “straw yellow,” and “pale horn gray”—are legible and appropriate. The line “Female, immature & nonbreeding male: yellowish to olive-green; dark wings & tail” is explicitly supported by Cornell, Animal Diversity Web, and Audubon.

The plate contains exactly one primary bird with one head, one beak, two anatomical wings, two legs, and one tail. The layout is readable and balanced, and no place name, ZIP code, coordinates, map, or local-observation detail appears.
